title: Radioactivity — alpha, beta and gamma radiation
examTip: Nuclear equations must balance on both sides. The total mass number on the left = the total mass number on the right. The same goes for atomic number. Always write the atomic and mass numbers for every particle, including the radiation given out.
introTips: An unstable nucleus gives out radiation to become more stable. Nothing outside triggers it, like heat or pressure. It happens randomly.
The three types of radiation differ a lot in how far they penetrate and how strongly they ionise. These two go in opposite directions.
Alpha is the most ionising but the least penetrating. Gamma is the least ionising but the most penetrating.
Nuclear equations use standard notation. The mass number goes on top and the atomic number on the bottom. The element symbol goes in the middle.
Background radiation is always present. It comes from natural and man-made sources. You are exposed to low levels every day.
intro: Radioactivity was found almost by accident. In 1896, Henri Becquerel left uranium salts on top of a photographic plate. He found the plate had been exposed, even in the dark. What was coming out of the uranium? It turned out to be different types of radiation. Each had very different properties and dangers, and in time, very different uses. Radioactivity has given us cancer treatments and nuclear power. It has also caused some of history's worst accidents. Knowing the difference between the three types is the essential starting point.

keyPoints.heading: Alpha radiation (α)
keyPoints.content: Some atomic nuclei are unstable. An unstable nucleus gives out radiation as it changes to become more stable. This is called radioactive decay. It is a random process. The activity of a source is the rate at which its unstable nuclei decay. It is measured in becquerels (Bq). A detector, such as a Geiger-Muller tube, counts the decays. The count-rate is the number of decays it records each second. The radiation given out may be an alpha particle, a beta particle, a gamma ray or a neutron. Alpha (α) radiation is a helium nucleus: 2 protons and 2 neutrons (mass number 4, atomic number 2). When a nucleus gives out an alpha particle, it loses 2 protons and 2 neutrons. The mass number falls by 4 and the atomic number falls by 2. This forms a new element. Nuclear equation notation: ⁴₂He. Properties: - stopped by a few centimetres of air or a sheet of paper - highly ionising: each alpha particle knocks many electrons off atoms as it travels, making lots of ions - short range in air (~5 cm) Danger: it is very dangerous inside the body (breathed in or swallowed), because it ionises so much. But outside the body, skin stops it easily. Example nuclear equation: radium-226 decays by alpha emission → radon-222: ²²⁶₈₈Ra → ²²²₈₆Rn + ⁴₂He.
writeBullets: Unstable nucleus → gives out radiation to become more stable. This is random
Activity — the rate of decay, in becquerels (Bq). Count-rate — decays recorded each second by a detector
The radiation may be an alpha particle, a beta particle, a gamma ray or a neutron
Alpha particle — 2 protons + 2 neutrons (a helium nucleus). Mass number 4, atomic number 2
After alpha emission, the mass number falls by 4 and the atomic number falls by 2
Stopped by paper or a few cm of air. The least penetrating
Highly ionising. It makes many ions along its path
Short range in air (~5 cm). Most dangerous if swallowed or breathed in

keyTerms.def: A helium nucleus (2 protons + 2 neutrons); emitted during alpha decay; highly ionising, stopped by paper
Radiation that knocks electrons off atoms, creating ions — alpha is the most ionising of the three types
The rate at which a source of unstable nuclei decays; measured in becquerels (Bq)
The number of decays recorded each second by a detector, such as a Geiger-Muller tube

keyPoints.memTip: Alpha = helium nucleus (⁴₂He). It loses 4 from the mass number and 2 from the atomic number.
keyPoints.tutor_note: Practise writing out alpha decay equations from scratch. Fill in the daughter nucleus numbers by subtraction.

keyPoints.heading: Beta radiation (β)
keyPoints.content: Beta (β) radiation is a fast-moving electron given out by the nucleus. A neutron in the nucleus turns into a proton plus an electron. The electron is given out as beta radiation. The nucleus gains one proton, so the atomic number goes up by 1. The mass number stays the same, because a neutron became a proton of the same mass. Nuclear notation: ⁰₋₁e (mass number 0, atomic number −1). Properties: - stopped by a few mm of aluminium (or about 1 m of air) - moderately ionising: less ionising than alpha, and more than gamma Example nuclear equation: carbon-14 decays by beta emission → nitrogen-14: ¹⁴₆C → ¹⁴₇N + ⁰₋₁e. Beta penetrates further than alpha, but ionises less.
writeBullets: Beta particle — a fast electron from the nucleus. Neutron → proton + electron
After beta emission, the mass number stays the same and the atomic number goes up by 1
Stopped by a few mm of aluminium or ~1 m of air
Moderately ionising. Less than alpha, more than gamma
Beta notation in equations: ⁰₋₁e

keyTerms.def: A fast electron emitted from the nucleus when a neutron converts to a proton; stopped by thin aluminium
A neutron in the nucleus converts to a proton, emitting a beta particle (electron) — atomic number increases by 1

keyPoints.memTip: Beta = a fast electron from the nucleus. The mass stays the same, and the atomic number goes up by 1.
keyPoints.tutor_note: Common mix-up: beta particles come FROM the nucleus. The nucleus does not already hold electrons. It makes them during the decay.

keyPoints.heading: Gamma radiation (γ)
keyPoints.content: Gamma (γ) radiation is electromagnetic radiation from the nucleus. It is made of high-frequency, high-energy waves. It has no mass and no charge. Gamma is often given out after alpha or beta decay. The nucleus does not change element when it gives out gamma. The mass number and atomic number both stay the same. Nuclear notation: ⁰₀γ. Properties: - never fully stopped, but greatly reduced by thick lead (several cm) or thick concrete (metres) - weakly ionising: it travels a long way through air and tissue. It ionises far fewer atoms than alpha or beta Danger: it can pass into the body and damage internal organs and DNA from outside. But it ionises less densely than alpha. Choosing the best radiation for a job: compare how far each type penetrates. Also compare its range in air and how strongly it ionises. For example, to detect radiation from inside the body, gamma is best. It passes out through the body to a detector. Alpha and beta would be absorbed by the body.
writeBullets: Gamma ray — electromagnetic radiation from the nucleus. No mass, no charge
After gamma emission, the mass number and atomic number both stay the same
Reduced (not fully stopped) by thick lead or thick concrete
Weakly ionising. It travels far, but ionises few atoms
Often given out alongside alpha or beta
To choose the best radiation for a use, compare penetration, range in air and ionising power

keyTerms.def: High-energy electromagnetic radiation emitted from the nucleus; no mass or charge; weakly ionising but very penetrating
Waves that travel at the speed of light; gamma rays are the highest energy part of the EM spectrum

keyPoints.memTip: Gamma = EM wave. No mass, no charge.
keyPoints.tutor_note: 'Stopped by lead' is not quite right. Gamma is only greatly reduced, not completely blocked.

keyPoints.heading: Background radiation and nuclear equations
keyPoints.content: Background radiation is low-level radiation that is always around us. It comes from natural and man-made sources. - Natural sources: radon gas from rocks (the largest source in the UK) and cosmic rays from space. Also food and drink, and rocks and buildings. - Man-made sources: medical X-rays, fallout from nuclear weapons testing, and nuclear accidents. The level you receive depends on where you live and on your job. Some rocks give out more radon than others. Some jobs, such as working with X-rays, add to your exposure. The radiation dose you receive is measured in sieverts (Sv). 1000 millisieverts (mSv) = 1 sievert (Sv). Writing nuclear equations: the mass numbers must balance on each side. So must the atomic numbers. - Alpha emission example: ²²⁶₈₈Ra → ²²²₈₆Rn + ⁴₂He. - Beta emission example: ¹⁴₆C → ¹⁴₇N + ⁰₋₁e. - Gamma emission: no change to the mass or atomic numbers. Steps: (1) write the parent nucleus; (2) write the radiation with its numbers; (3) balance the remaining numbers to find the daughter nucleus.
writeBullets: Background radiation — always present. Natural: radon gas, cosmic rays, food and drink. Man-made: fallout, nuclear accidents, medical X-rays
Nuclear equations: mass numbers must balance, and atomic numbers must balance
Alpha: mass number −4, atomic number −2 in daughter nucleus
Beta: mass number unchanged, atomic number +1 in daughter nucleus
Gamma: no change to the mass or atomic number. The nucleus only loses energy
Background level and dose depend on where you live and on your job. Dose is measured in sieverts (Sv)

keyTerms.def: Low-level radiation from natural and man-made sources always present in the environment
An equation showing radioactive decay with mass numbers and atomic numbers balanced on both sides
The unit of radiation dose; 1000 millisieverts (mSv) = 1 sievert (Sv)

keyPoints.memTip: Balance the top numbers, then balance the bottom numbers. Radon is the biggest source of background radiation in the UK.
keyPoints.tutor_note: Practise completing nuclear equations where the daughter nucleus is unknown. This is the most common calculation in this topic.

tables.title: Comparison of alpha, beta and gamma radiation
rows: Reduced by thick lead or concrete
No change to atomic or mass number

0.question: Which particles make up an alpha particle?
0.correctFeedback: Correct! An alpha particle is a helium nucleus: 2 protons + 2 neutrons. That gives mass number 4 and atomic number 2.
0.wrongFeedback: An alpha particle is a helium nucleus: 2 protons and 2 neutrons. Mass number = 4, atomic number = 2. It has no electrons.

1.question: Which type of radiation is stopped by a few millimetres of aluminium?
1.correctFeedback: Correct! Beta radiation (fast electrons) is stopped by a few mm of aluminium. Alpha is stopped by paper. Gamma needs thick lead to be greatly reduced.
1.wrongFeedback: Beta radiation is stopped by a few mm of aluminium. Alpha is stopped by paper (or a few cm of air). Gamma is only greatly reduced by thick lead or concrete.

2.question: A nucleus gives out a gamma ray. What happens to its mass number and atomic number?
options: The mass number falls by 4 and the atomic number falls by 2
The mass number stays the same and the atomic number goes up by 1
2.correctFeedback: Correct! A gamma ray has no mass and no charge. So the nucleus keeps the same mass number and atomic number.
2.wrongFeedback: A gamma ray has no mass and no charge. So both numbers stay the same. Alpha lowers them by 4 and 2. Beta raises the atomic number by 1.

3.question: Radon-222 (²²²₈₆Rn) decays by alpha emission. What is the atomic number of the daughter nucleus?
3.correctFeedback: Correct! In alpha emission, the atomic number falls by 2. 86 − 2 = 84. The new nucleus has mass number 218.
3.wrongFeedback: Alpha emission removes 2 protons from the nucleus. So the atomic number falls by 2: 86 − 2 = 84. The mass number also falls by 4: 222 − 4 = 218.

commonMistakes: Mixing up ionising power and penetrating power. Alpha is the most ionising but least penetrating. Gamma is the least ionising but most penetrating. These go in opposite directions.
Saying beta particles come from the electron shells. They are made in the nucleus when a neutron turns into a proton. Then they are given out.
In nuclear equations, forgetting that the atomic numbers must balance too. Most people remember the mass numbers but forget to check the bottom numbers.
Saying gamma is 'stopped by lead'. It is greatly reduced but not fully blocked. A common phrase is 'absorbed by thick lead'.
Mixing up the effect on the nucleus. Alpha lowers both the mass number (−4) and the atomic number (−2). Beta raises the atomic number (+1) but leaves the mass number unchanged. Gamma changes neither.
examTips: For nuclear equations, check that the top numbers (mass numbers) and bottom numbers (atomic numbers) both balance on each side. This earns you both marks.
When comparing types of radiation, link ionising power and penetrating power together. More ionising means it loses energy faster, so it penetrates less far.

Questions about hazards want you to say two things. Inside the body, alpha is most dangerous, because it ionises nearby cells strongly. Outside the body, gamma is most dangerous, because it reaches internal organs.
Radon gas is the largest source of background radiation in the UK. It often comes up in 'state a source of background radiation' questions.
To choose the best radiation for a use, compare penetration, range in air and ionising power. Say why the other types would not work.
revisionCardBullets: Unstable nuclei give out radiation to become more stable. Decay is random
Activity in becquerels (Bq). Count-rate = decays recorded each second by a detector
Radiation can be an alpha particle, a beta particle, a gamma ray or a neutron
Alpha: helium nucleus (2p + 2n). Mass 4, charge +2. Stopped by paper. Most ionising
Alpha decay: mass number −4, atomic number −2
Beta: fast electron from the nucleus. Mass 0, charge −1. Stopped by aluminium. Moderately ionising
Beta decay: neutron → proton + electron. Atomic number +1, mass number unchanged
Gamma: EM wave. No mass, no charge. Reduced by thick lead. Least ionising, most penetrating
Gamma emission: no change to mass number or atomic number
Nuclear equations: both mass numbers and atomic numbers must balance
Background radiation: natural (radon gas, cosmic rays, food, buildings) and man-made (fallout, nuclear accidents, medical X-rays)
Alpha is most dangerous inside the body. Gamma is most dangerous from outside the body
Ionising power: α > β > γ. Penetrating power: γ > β > α
